cards.front: What is a brake, in terms of energy?
cards.back: A heat conversion machine that works exactly opposite to an engine. Brakes convert the energy of motion back into the energy of heat through friction between the brake drums or rotors and the brake linings or pads.

cards.front: What is the final factor in stopping (and moving) a vehicle?
cards.back: The contact between the vehicle and the road through the tires. Even though the energy of motion turns the wheels, the vehicle won't go anywhere unless there's traction between the tires and the road surface. Bald or defective tires may degrade braking performance.

cards.front: How is brake heat dissipated?
cards.back: The heat is absorbed and dissipated into the atmosphere, primarily through the brake drums/rotors.

cards.front: How much stopping force does a loaded tractor-trailer need for an emergency stop from 100 km/h?
cards.back: A combination weighing up to 63,500 kg might take over one kilometre and over one minute to accelerate to 100 km/h, but in an emergency might have to stop in as little as seven seconds — roughly 1/9 of that time. That requires a stopping force of nine times the acceleration force — the equivalent of approximately 4,000 hp.

cards.front: What happens if one or two brakes on a combination are out of adjustment?
cards.back: The other brakes have to do more than their share of the braking, resulting in a longer stopping distance. They may work harder than they're manufactured to, building up more heat than they can absorb and dissipate — too much heat can result in brake damage and possible failure.

cards.front: What makes up total stopping distance (or total stopping time)?
cards.back: Driver's perception time + reaction time + brake lag time + braking time. You see a hazard, think (decide to stop), then do (apply the brake).

cards.front: How long are perception time, reaction time and air brake lag time?
cards.back: About 3/4 of a second of perception time (see-think), another 3/4 of a second of reaction time (do), and approximately 4/10 of a second of brake lag between when you apply the brake and when the air brakes begin to function.

cards.front: What following distance should drivers of buses, trucks and other large heavy vehicles keep?
cards.back: Never less than five seconds behind the vehicle ahead at highway speeds. Stay even further back when conditions are less than ideal. (Passenger cars and light trucks use the two-second rule.)

cards.front: How does doubling speed or weight affect the stopping power required?
cards.back: 2 x vehicle speed requires 4 x the stopping power. 2 x vehicle weight requires 2 x the stopping power. 2 x speed and 2 x weight together require 8 x the stopping power.

cards.front: How does the grade of the road affect stopping distance?
cards.back: A vehicle travelling down a hill needs a longer stopping distance than at the same speed on a level surface because of the effect of gravity. A vehicle travelling up a hill will stop in a shorter distance.

cards.front: What temperatures can brake components handle?
cards.back: In normal stopping, brake components heat up to about 120 degrees C (almost 250 degrees F). They can handle up to about 250 degrees C under hard braking. Beyond that, heat can cause brake fade, brake damage and/or brake failure — components or tires may actually catch fire.

cards.front: What is brake fade and what causes it?
cards.back: Brake fade occurs when your brakes stop working properly because they're overheated — the vehicle takes longer to stop, or may not stop at all. As brake drums heat up they expand away from the brake linings. It's caused by excessive hard or frequent braking without enough cooling time — in other words, poor speed control.

cards.front: What are retarders and what are the four main types?
cards.back: Retarders provide auxiliary slowing of the vehicle, such as controlling speed on long downgrades without using the main braking system, saving the brakes for emergency stopping. The four main types: engine retarders, exhaust retarders, hydraulic driveline retarders and electric driveline retarders. Many can absorb as much or more horsepower than the engine can develop.

cards.front: How should you use an engine retarder, and when should you be cautious?
cards.back: An engine retarder is more efficient at a higher engine r.p.m. and a lower vehicle speed, so select the right gear before you start down a hill. Be cautious on slippery road surfaces — some retarders can cause the drive wheels to lock up, stalling the engine, causing loss of control or even a tractor/trailer jackknife. Obey municipal signs restricting engine retarder use.

cards.front: How do you brake on icy roads (without ABS)?
cards.back: Use extremely light pressure on the brake to control speed and help prevent the wheels from locking up. A slowly revolving wheel on an icy surface is more effective than a locked wheel skidding. You need snow tires and/or chains on icy roads; in extremely bad conditions, parking the vehicle may be safer than driving.

cards.front: What is the correct technique for descending a long downgrade?
cards.back: Select a safe speed for your vehicle's weight, length, steepness of grade, weather and road conditions. Be in a lower gear than you used to climb the hill, use the vehicle's retarding device, and never shift to a higher gear on a downgrade unless the speed can be controlled by a retarding device or engine compression. If speed still increases: apply the brakes hard enough to reduce speed by 10 to 15 km/h, then downshift to a lower main gear (don't use the splitter valve for shifting on a downhill). Keep the vehicle in gear all the way down.

cards.front: How do you handle water on the roadway?
cards.back: Water can reduce braking efficiency. Reduce speed before large pools of water, cover the brake pedal as you approach, and place a slight drag (slight constant pressure) on the brakes while driving through — this reduces the amount of water entering the brake drums and shoes. Afterwards, test the brakes with slight pedal pressure for a short distance to dry them out.

cards.front: What are runaway lanes for?
cards.back: Runaway lanes are located beside the road on some downhill grades to help slow and stop vehicles if their brakes fail going downhill. Use them only to control your speed or stop — don't use them for any other purpose.

cards.front: What are the key facts about ABS on heavy vehicles?
cards.back: ABS is mandatory in Canada on all trucks and buses over 4,560 kg manufactured since April 1, 2000, and on all commercial trailers equipped with air brakes. It helps prevent wheel lockup or skids from overbraking on slippery surfaces and may help prevent jackknifing — but it doesn't let you drive faster or stop sooner, and on some surfaces such as gravel the braking distance may be longer. In an emergency: apply firm, hard continuous pressure and don't pump the brakes. If tractor and trailers don't all have ABS, brake as if the combination has no ABS.

cards.front: What is Automatic Traction Control (ATC)?
cards.back: An optional addition to an ABS system. Using the same wheel sensors as ABS, ATC senses if a drive wheel has lost traction and is spinning; it applies that wheel's brake, transferring power to the opposite side. In extremely slippery conditions it reduces engine power so the wheels can regain traction. Most ATC-equipped vehicles have a dashboard decal and a dash-mounted lamp that lights if wheel spin occurs.

questions.q: What is the final factor that determines whether a vehicle will move?
choices: The horsepower of the engine
Traction between the tires and the road surface
The gear ratio of the transmission
The weight of the load
questions.explanation: Even though the energy of motion turns the vehicle's wheels, the vehicle won't go anywhere unless there's traction between the tires and the road surface.

questions.q: In terms of energy, what do brakes do?
choices: Convert heat energy into the energy of motion
Store the energy of motion in the brake drums
Convert electrical energy into stopping force
Convert the energy of motion into the energy of heat through friction
questions.explanation: A brake is a heat conversion machine that works exactly opposite to an engine — it converts the energy of motion back into heat through friction between the drums/rotors and the linings/pads.

questions.q: How is brake heat dissipated?
choices: It is absorbed and dissipated into the atmosphere, primarily through the brake drums/rotors
It is carried away by the brake fluid
It is absorbed by the tires
It is vented through the exhaust system
questions.explanation: The heat created by braking is absorbed and dissipated into the atmosphere, primarily through the brake drums/rotors.

questions.q: How much can a heavy tractor-trailer combination weigh when loaded?
choices: Up to 28,000 kg
Up to 40,500 kg
Up to 63,500 kg
Up to 25,000 kg
questions.explanation: A heavy tractor-trailer combination can weigh up to 63,500 kg when loaded.

questions.q: Stopping a tractor-trailer combination from 100 km/h in an emergency (about seven seconds) requires a stopping force equivalent to approximately how much horsepower?
choices: 400 hp
120 hp
questions.explanation: Stopping that quickly requires a stopping force of nine times the acceleration force — the equivalent of approximately 4,000 hp.

questions.q: What happens when one or two brakes on a 16-brake tractor-trailer combination are out of adjustment?
choices: The other brakes must do more than their share, resulting in a longer stopping distance and possible overheating
Nothing noticeable — 14 brakes are more than enough
The vehicle stops faster because the remaining brakes grip harder
Only the trailer's stopping ability is affected
questions.explanation: If one or two brakes aren't correctly adjusted, the others have to do more than their share, resulting in a longer stopping distance and possible heat buildup, brake damage and failure.

questions.q: What is an average driver's reaction time?
choices: About 2 seconds
About 4/10 of a second
About 1/4 of a second
About 3/4 of a second
questions.explanation: An average driver's reaction time is about 3/4 of a second — the time between recognizing a hazard ahead and applying the brakes.

questions.q: What makes up total stopping time for a vehicle with air brakes?
choices: Reaction time plus braking time
Perception time plus braking time
Perception time + reaction time + brake lag time + braking time
Brake lag time plus braking time
questions.explanation: Total stopping time (or distance) is the driver's perception time plus reaction time plus brake lag time plus braking time.

questions.q: What is brake lag time in an air brake system?
choices: The approximately 4/10 of a second between when you apply the brake and when the brakes begin to function
The time it takes to recognize a hazard
The 3/4 of a second it takes to move your foot to the brake pedal
The time the vehicle travels after the brakes engage until it stops
questions.explanation: Unlike a car's brakes, which begin to work almost instantly, air brakes have a brake lag time of approximately 4/10 of a second between application and when the brakes begin to function.

questions.q: At highway speeds, how far behind the vehicle ahead should drivers of buses, trucks and other large heavy vehicles stay?
choices: At least two seconds
Never less than five seconds
At least three seconds
One vehicle length per 10 km/h
questions.explanation: Drivers of buses, trucks and other large heavy vehicles should never be less than five seconds behind the vehicle ahead at highway speeds; the two-second rule is for passenger cars and light trucks.

questions.q: What is the most common air brake system defect found during a commercial vehicle inspection?
choices: Leaking air lines
Worn brake linings
Brakes that are out of adjustment
A faulty compressor
questions.explanation: The most common air brake system defect found during a commercial vehicle inspection is brakes that are out of adjustment.

questions.q: If the speed of a vehicle is doubled, how much stopping power is required?
choices: Two times the stopping power
Eight times the stopping power
The same stopping power
Four times the stopping power
questions.explanation: Two times the vehicle speed requires four times the stopping power.

questions.q: If the weight of the vehicle is doubled, how many times must the stopping power be increased?
choices: Two times
Four times
Eight times
It doesn't change
questions.explanation: Two times the vehicle weight requires two times the stopping power.

questions.q: If both the speed and the weight of a vehicle are doubled, how much stopping power is required?
choices: Four times the stopping power
Eight times the stopping power
Two times the stopping power
Six times the stopping power
questions.explanation: Two times the vehicle speed and two times the vehicle weight together require eight times the stopping power.

questions.q: Compared to stopping on a level surface at the same speed, a vehicle travelling down a hill will need:
choices: A shorter stopping distance
The same stopping distance
Less brake pressure
A longer stopping distance, because of the effect of gravity
questions.explanation: A vehicle travelling down a hill needs a longer stopping distance than one travelling the same speed on a level surface because of the effect of gravity; travelling uphill it stops in a shorter distance.

questions.q: What temperature do brake components reach in normal stopping, and what is the most they should handle?
choices: About 250 degrees C in normal stopping, up to 500 degrees C under hard braking
About 50 degrees C in normal stopping, up to 120 degrees C under hard braking
About 120 degrees C in normal stopping, up to about 250 degrees C under hard braking
About 100 degrees C in normal stopping, up to 200 degrees C under hard braking
questions.explanation: In normal stopping, brake components heat up to about 120 degrees C (almost 250 degrees F) and can handle up to about 250 degrees C under hard braking.

questions.q: What causes brake fade?
choices: Overheated brakes — as brake drums heat up they expand away from the brake linings, so the brakes stop working properly
Water washing away the brake fluid
Cold brakes on a winter morning
Brake linings that are too new
questions.explanation: Brake fade occurs when brakes stop working properly because they're overheated; as brake drums heat up, they expand away from the brake linings, so the vehicle takes longer to stop or may not stop at all.

questions.q: What are the four main types of retarders?
choices: Air, hydraulic, vacuum and electric retarders
Drum, disc, wedge and air retarders
Engine, exhaust, hydraulic driveline and electric driveline retarders
Compression, friction, magnetic and gravity retarders
questions.explanation: The four main types of retarders are engine retarders, exhaust retarders, hydraulic driveline retarders and electric driveline retarders.

questions.q: When is an engine retarder most efficient?
choices: At a low engine r.p.m. and a high vehicle speed
At a higher engine r.p.m. and a lower vehicle speed
Only when the vehicle is in its top gear
Only when the service brakes are applied at the same time
questions.explanation: An engine retarder is more efficient at a higher engine r.p.m. and a lower vehicle speed, so it's important to select the right gear before you start down a hill.

questions.q: Why should you be cautious using retarders or engine brakes on slippery road surfaces?
choices: They drain the air pressure from the brake system
They only work above 80 km/h
They can overheat the engine
Some can cause the drive wheels to lock up, stalling the engine, which can result in loss of control or a jackknife
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, some retarders/engine brakes can cause the drive wheels to lock up, stalling the engine, resulting in loss of control or even causing a tractor/trailer to jackknife.

questions.q: How should you brake on icy roads in a vehicle without ABS?
choices: Use extremely light pressure on the brake — a slowly revolving wheel is more effective than a locked wheel skidding
Apply firm, hard continuous pressure until the vehicle stops
Pump the brakes rapidly to break up the ice
Apply only the trailer brakes
questions.explanation: On icy roads, use extremely light pressure on the brake to control speed and prevent wheel lockup; a slowly revolving wheel on ice is more effective than a locked wheel skidding.

questions.q: If your speed keeps increasing on a downgrade despite engine compression and your retarding device, what should you do?
choices: Shift to a higher gear to let the engine catch up
Apply the brakes hard enough to reduce speed by 10 to 15 km/h, then downshift to a lower main gear (don't use the splitter valve on a downhill)
Ride the brakes lightly all the way down the hill
Shift into neutral and use the service brakes only
questions.explanation: If speed increases above your chosen speed, apply the brakes hard enough to reduce speed by 10 to 15 km/h while the brakes are cold, downshift to a lower main gear without using the splitter valve, and repeat if needed — keeping the vehicle in gear all the way down.

questions.q: What should you do with the brakes when you must drive through a large amount of water on the roadway?
choices: Pump the brakes rapidly while in the water
Avoid touching the brakes until you're through the water
Place a slight drag (slight constant pressure) on the brakes to reduce the amount of water entering the brake drums and shoes
Apply the parking brake lightly
questions.explanation: Cover the brake pedal as you approach and place a slight drag on the brakes while driving through water — the slight drag reduces the amount of water entering the brake drums and shoes. Afterwards, dry the brakes with slight pedal pressure for a short distance.

questions.q: ABS is mandatory in Canada on which vehicles?
choices: All commercial vehicles regardless of age or weight
Only tractor units manufactured since 2010
Trucks and buses over 4,600 kg manufactured since 1995
All trucks and buses over 4,560 kg manufactured since April 1, 2000, and all commercial trailers equipped with air brakes
questions.explanation: ABS is mandatory in Canada on all trucks and buses over 4,560 kg manufactured since April 1, 2000 and on all commercial trailers equipped with air brakes.

questions.q: What is the correct emergency stopping technique with ABS?
choices: Apply firm, hard continuous pressure to the brake pedal until the vehicle stops — don't pump the brakes
Pump the brakes to keep the system engaged
Apply light pressure and release when you feel the pedal shudder
Apply the trailer brakes first, then the tractor brakes
questions.explanation: With ABS, apply firm, hard continuous pressure until the vehicle stops; pumping the brakes turns the system on and off, and brake noise, pedal movement or shudder is normal.

questions.q: On slippery roads, what can happen if you apply brake pressure too forcefully or apply only the trailer brakes of a combination vehicle?
choices: The brakes will automatically release to protect the system
The trailer will slow smoothly while the tractor keeps its speed
The wheels may lock up, which can result in a skid or jackknife
Nothing, because all the brakes apply at the same time and pressure
questions.explanation: Applying brake pressure too forcefully or only applying the trailer brakes on slippery roads may cause the wheels to lock up, which can result in a skid or jackknife — use extra caution when applying brakes in a curve.

questions.q: With Automatic Traction Control (ATC), what happens when a drive wheel begins to spin on a slippery surface?
choices: All of the drive wheels are locked until traction returns
The trailer brakes are applied to straighten the combination
Engine power is increased to force the wheel to grip
The system applies that wheel's brake, transferring power to the opposite side — and in extremely slippery conditions it reduces engine power so the wheels can regain traction
questions.explanation: ATC uses the ABS wheel sensors to detect a spinning drive wheel; it applies that brake, transferring power to the opposite side, and in extremely slippery conditions reduces engine power to let the wheels regain traction.
